meta.description: Training data for the intent classifier and source of the question buttons shown in the interface. Each intent carries a display string that is excluded from its own patterns, so classifying a button click is a genuine generalisation rather than a lookup.

meta.show_when: always means the question is offered at any time. after_assessment means it is offered only once a person has been scored.

intents.display: What can you help me with?
responses: I can explain any prediction this model makes, break down which attributes drove it, describe how the model was built and evaluated, and set out where it should not be trusted.
Ask me about a prediction and its reasoning, about the algorithm and its accuracy, about the census data behind it, or about the fairness problems it carries.
Four areas: the current assessment, the explanation behind it, the model and its evaluation, and the limitations of the whole thing.

patterns: how do you know what mattered
where do these numbers come from
how are the contributions worked out
how do you calculate each contribution
responses: The contributions come from TreeSHAP, built into the algorithm itself. They are exact rather than estimated: the contributions plus the model's baseline add up to the raw output, and converting that sum gives back the probability precisely. The unit is log odds, not a percentage.

This is not a simplified stand-in model guessing at reasons. Each figure is the attribute's exact share of the raw output, and they reconcile to the prediction to within rounding error. They are measured in log odds.

The algorithm can report exactly how much each attribute moved its own output. Those values sum to the prediction, which is why the breakdown can be checked rather than trusted. Values are in log odds, so a contribution of 0.8 does not mean eighty percent.
{model_name}, a gradient boosted tree ensemble, trained on {train_rows} census records with {features} prepared features.
The prediction comes from {model_name} fitted to {train_rows} records. It was chosen after comparing eight algorithms.
{model_name}. It builds many shallow decision trees in sequence, each correcting the previous ones.
{accuracy_pct} accurate on {test_rows} held-out records it never saw during training. It is wrong roughly one time in eight.
On the held-out file it reaches {accuracy_pct} accuracy with an area under the curve of {roc_auc}. That leaves a substantial error rate.
{accuracy_pct} on data held back from training. Accuracy alone flatters it, because most people in the data fall below the threshold anyway.

Recall is {recall_pct}, so roughly a third of upper bracket cases are missed. Precision is {precision_pct} when it does predict the upper bracket.
F1 of {f1}, from precision {precision_pct} and recall {recall_pct}. The recall figure is the weaker of the two and matters most if missing someone is costly.

intents.display: Why this algorithm and not another?
patterns: why did you pick that one
what about a neural network instead
why choose this one and not something else
responses: Eight algorithms were compared on the same split and {model_name} scored highest, so it was deployed. The cost is that a tree ensemble has no coefficients to read, which is why the explanation uses exact attribution instead.

It won the comparison. A simpler model such as logistic regression would be easier to read directly, but the gap in performance was real and the attribution method recovers the explanation without approximating it.

{model_name} performed best of the eight tested. The interpretability that a linear model would have given for free is recovered through the contribution breakdown, which is exact rather than an estimate.

patterns: can i read the score as a chance
do the probabilities actually mean anything
responses: Yes, and it was measured rather than assumed. The Brier score is {brier} and the average gap between predicted and observed rates is {ece}, so a prediction of seventy percent does correspond to roughly seventy percent of such cases falling above the threshold.
Checked on the validation split: average calibration error {ece}, Brier score {brier}. Boosted models often distort probabilities, and this one does not do so badly enough to affect the bands.
The reliability curve tracks the diagonal closely, with a Brier score of {brier}. That is why the bands can be built on the probability rather than on the raw ranking.
